# Geodesic methods {#geodesic}

*If the data lie on a folded sheet, how do you flatten it back out?*

Every method in this chapter follows the same two-step recipe. Estimate a metric
on the sample, then embed that metric in the plane. Isomap, Laplacian eigenmaps,
diffusion maps and locally linear embedding differ only in which metric they
estimate and how they embed it, and all four estimate it from the same object: a
$k$-nearest-neighbour graph built in the ambient space.

That shared dependence is what makes the family unusually easy to audit on a
rigid fold. Rigid folding is an isometry (Chapter \@ref(folding-geometry)), so
the folded surface carries the metric of the flat sheet unchanged. Geodesic
distances, the Laplace–Beltrami operator, and the local affine charts that LLE
fits are all identical at $\theta = 0$ and at $\theta_{\max}$. Whatever any of
these methods would return *given the true metric*, it would return identically
at every fold angle. The population target is $\theta$-invariant.

So every bit of $\theta$-dependence in the curves below is graph-construction
error. Nothing else is available to cause it. This is the sharpest statement the
benchmark supports, and it is the reason this chapter is longer than its
neighbours.

## Classical MDS as the baseline

`cmdscale()` double-centres a squared-distance matrix, takes its leading
eigenvectors, and scales them by the square roots of the eigenvalues. Applied to
a Euclidean distance matrix it returns the principal component scores up to sign
— it is Chapter \@ref(linear)'s PCA, re-expressed in the vocabulary the rest of
this chapter uses. That is precisely its value here: it holds the embedding step
fixed so that the distance matrix is the only thing that varies.

```{r geo-cmdscale}
library(foldbench)

pat <- miura_ori(n_rows = 6, n_cols = 6, a = 1, b = 1, alpha = pi / 3)
fld <- fold(pat, theta = 0.8)
s   <- sample_manifold(pat, theta = 0.8, n = 800, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])

Y_mds <- cmdscale(dist(s$X), k = 2)
reconstruction_error(Y_mds, s$truth)

# cmdscale on Euclidean distances is PCA
Y_pca <- prcomp(s$X, rank. = 2)$x
max(abs(abs(cor(Y_mds, Y_pca)) - diag(2)))
```

At $\theta = 0$ ambient and geodesic distances coincide and the baseline is exact
to machine precision. Folding then contracts the sheet *anisotropically* in
$\mathbb{R}^3$: the corrugation direction is squashed by a factor
$\lambda(\theta) < 1$, the transverse direction by a different factor. Procrustes
alignment permits rotation, reflection and a single isotropic scale, so it can
absorb neither. `reconstruction_error` therefore rises monotonically with $\theta$,
and that curve is the floor every method below has to beat.

## Isomap

Isomap replaces the ambient distance matrix with shortest-path distances on the
neighbourhood graph and hands the result to the same `cmdscale`
[@tenenbaum2000isomap]. Written out, it is four lines.

```{r geo-knn-graph}
knn_graph <- function(X, k) {
  D  <- as.matrix(dist(X))
  nn <- t(apply(D, 1, function(d) order(d)[2:(k + 1)]))
  el <- cbind(rep(seq_len(nrow(X)), each = k), as.vector(t(nn)))
  g  <- igraph::simplify(igraph::graph_from_edgelist(el, directed = FALSE))
  igraph::E(g)$weight <- D[igraph::as_edgelist(g)]
  g
}

isomap_embed <- function(X, k, d = 2) {
  g <- knn_graph(X, k)
  if (igraph::components(g)$no > 1L) return(NULL)   # fragmented graph
  Dg <- igraph::distances(g, algorithm = "dijkstra")
  cmdscale(Dg, k = d)
}
```

`vegan::isomap()` does the same thing with more care about edge cases, and
`vegan::isomapdist()` returns the graph distance matrix on its own, which is what
the decomposition below needs. Two of its arguments matter. `epsilon` builds an
$\varepsilon$-ball graph instead of a $k$-nearest-neighbour graph; on a sheet
sampled at uniform density the two are close, but $\varepsilon$-balls fragment
more readily near the boundary. And `fragmentedOK = FALSE` — the default — makes
a disconnected graph an error rather than silently embedding the largest
component. Leave it at the default. A run that quietly discards a third of the
sheet and reports a low reconstruction error is worse than a run that stops.

```{r geo-isomap-vegan}
Dg <- vegan::isomapdist(dist(s$X), k = 12)
Y_iso <- cmdscale(Dg, k = 2)
reconstruction_error(Y_iso, s$truth)
```

Cost is $O(n^2)$ memory for the distance matrix and $O(n^2 \log n)$ for
all-pairs Dijkstra, which caps the sample size at a few thousand before landmark
variants become necessary.

## Locally linear embedding

LLE takes the opposite view: never estimate a global metric at all
[@roweis2000lle]. For each point, find the affine weights $w_{ij}$ over its $k$
neighbours that best reconstruct it, constrained to sum to one; then find the
low-dimensional configuration that the *same* weights reconstruct as well as
possible [@saul2003think]. The sum-to-one constraint makes the weights invariant
to translation, rotation and scaling of the neighbourhood, which is the sense in
which LLE never needs a metric.

What it assumes is that each neighbourhood is well approximated by an affine
subspace of the intended output dimension. On a piecewise-flat surface that
assumption is not approximately true, it is either exactly true or badly false.
In the interior of a facet the neighbourhood *is* affine and the weights are
exact. At a crease the neighbourhood spans two planes, its affine hull is
three-dimensional, and the reconstruction has a two-parameter family of exact
solutions. The creases are therefore exactly where the regularisation decides
the answer.

The CRAN `lle` package is archived, so the book implements the algorithm
directly. Twenty lines, and having them on the page makes the dependence on
`reg` visible instead of buried.

```{r geo-lle}
lle_embed <- function(X, k = 12, d = 2, reg = 1e-3) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  D <- as.matrix(dist(X))
  W <- matrix(0, n, n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    nb <- order(D[i, ])[2:(k + 1)]
    Z  <- sweep(X[nb, , drop = FALSE], 2, X[i, ])
    C  <- tcrossprod(Z)
    C  <- C + reg * sum(diag(C)) * diag(k)   # k > ambient dim: C is singular
    w  <- solve(C, rep(1, k))
    W[i, nb] <- w / sum(w)
  }
  M <- crossprod(diag(n) - W)
  e <- RSpectra::eigs_sym(M, k = d + 1, sigma = 0)   # shift-invert at zero
  e$vectors[, order(e$values)][, 2:(d + 1), drop = FALSE]
}
```

The regularisation is not a numerical nicety. The local Gram matrix $C$ is
$k \times k$ but has rank at most $D$, the ambient dimension. Here $D = 3$ and
$k$ is in the dozens, so $C$ is singular by a wide margin at every point on the
sheet, the weights are non-unique, and `reg` alone selects among them. Vary
`reg` over three orders of magnitude and the embedding changes visibly. That is
the standing instability of LLE, and this benchmark puts it in its worst regime:
a two-dimensional manifold in three dimensions, where $k$ exceeds $D$ for any
usable neighbourhood size. The second eigenproblem is delicate for a related
reason — the bottom eigenvector of $M$ is the constant vector with eigenvalue
zero, and the gap to the next one is small, so the shift-invert solve above is
the minimum required care.

## What Isomap's error is made of

Isomap's premise is this book's premise: recover the geodesic metric, then embed
it. On a rigid fold the geodesic metric is known in closed form, so the premise
can be checked rather than assumed. Provided the flat crease pattern is
intrinsically convex — true for the rectangular Miura sheet, false as soon as the
pattern has a hole or a re-entrant boundary — the straight segment between any
two points of the flat sheet stays inside it, and the geodesic distance on the
folded surface is exactly the Euclidean distance between the corresponding rows
of the ground-truth unfolding.

```{r geo-truth-identity}
# Folding is an isometry, so the exact geodesic distance between two samples is
# the Euclidean distance between their rows of the flat truth. There is nothing
# to estimate and nothing to converge to: this is the answer key, in closed form.
D_true <- dist(s$truth)

# The ambient metric can only understate the surface separation, never overstate
# it. The largest gap is the worst short circuit in the sample.
max(as.matrix(dist(s$X)) - as.matrix(D_true))   # <= 0 up to rounding
max(as.matrix(D_true) - as.matrix(dist(s$X)))   # the worst short circuit
```

That identity splits Isomap's error into two pieces, and the split is
measurable, which it is not on any other benchmark:

$$
\underbrace{\hat{d}_{ij}}_{\text{graph}} \;=\;
\underbrace{d_{\mathcal{M}}(i,j)}_{\text{truth}} \;+\;
\underbrace{\big(\hat{d}_{ij} - d_{\mathcal{M}}(i,j)\big)}_{\text{estimation error}},
\qquad
Y \;=\; \operatorname{cmdscale}(\hat{D}, 2).
$$

Feed `cmdscale` the exact geodesics and the second term vanishes. But $D_{\text{true}}$
is the distance matrix of a set of points that already lie in a plane, so it is
exactly Euclidean of rank two, its double-centring has exactly two non-zero
eigenvalues, and classical MDS reconstructs $\mathcal{U}$ up to a rigid motion.
The embedding step contributes *nothing*.

```{r geo-decomposition}
reconstruction_error(cmdscale(D_true, k = 2), s$truth)   # ~1e-15: embedding error is zero
reconstruction_error(cmdscale(Dg,     k = 2), s$truth)   # all of Isomap's error

rel_err <- function(A, B) sqrt(sum((A - B)^2) / sum(B^2))
rel_err(as.matrix(Dg), as.matrix(D_true))       # graph estimation error
```

So on a rigid fold, one hundred per cent of Isomap's reconstruction error is
graph-estimation error. There is no residual "MDS cannot represent this"
term to hide behind, and no need to argue about how much of the failure belongs
to which stage.

One refinement makes the accounting sharper still. Graph distances are biased
*upward*: a polygonal chain of hops is never shorter than the straight line it
approximates, and the bias vanishes as the sample density grows
[@bernstein2000graph]. But `reconstruction_error` aligns scale, so a bias that is
uniform across all pairs costs exactly nothing. Only *anisotropic* distortion is
charged. This is why the honest part of the graph error stays invisible for a
long stretch of $\theta$ — and why short circuits, which contract one direction
and leave the other alone, are charged at full price the moment they appear.

## Short circuits

Define, for each edge of the graph, the distortion ratio

$$\rho_{ij} \;=\; \frac{d_{\mathcal{M}}(i,j)}{\lVert x_i - x_j \rVert}\;\ge\;1 ,$$

the factor by which an edge understates the true surface separation of its
endpoints. On a flat sheet $\rho \equiv 1$. Within a facet $\rho = 1$ exactly, at
any $\theta$. An edge is a **short circuit** when $\rho_{ij} > \tau$ for a
threshold $\tau$; the book uses $\tau = 2$, meaning the edge claims as
neighbours two points at least twice as far apart along the surface as through
the air. Computing $\rho$ requires the answer key, which is the point.

```{r geo-shortcircuit-flag}
short_circuits <- function(g, X, U, tau = 2) {
  el  <- igraph::as_edgelist(g)
  amb <- sqrt(rowSums((X[el[, 1], ] - X[el[, 2], ])^2))
  geo <- sqrt(rowSums((U[el[, 1], ] - U[el[, 2], ])^2))   # exact, by isometry
  data.frame(i = el[, 1], j = el[, 2],
             ambient = amb, geodesic = geo,
             rho = geo / amb, short = geo / amb > tau)
}
```

The mechanism is the one Chapter \@ref(generative) previews. As $\theta$ grows,
facets that are far apart along the surface approach one another in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, the ambient $k$-nearest-neighbour search stops respecting the
surface, and the graph acquires edges that jump the fold. Isomap's response is
not graceful, for a structural reason: Dijkstra takes a *minimum* over paths, so
a single bad edge is enough to corrupt every pair whose shortest path can be
routed through it. The damage is not proportional to the number of bad edges.

```{r geo-shortcircuit-map, fig.height=3.6, fig.alt="Two panels of the same k-nearest-neighbour graph on a folded Miura sheet at a fold angle just past onset. Left panel shows the folded surface seen side-on in the x-z plane; right panel shows the exact flat unfolding. Graph edges are drawn as line segments, with honest edges as thin solid lines in dark purple and short-circuit edges as dashed orange lines. In the left panel the short-circuit edges are short and inconspicuous, spanning the narrow gap between adjacent facets. In the right panel the same edges are revealed as long chords running across the sheet, connecting regions that are far apart on the true manifold."}
s2 <- sample_manifold(pat, theta = 1.15, n = 800, seed = BENCH_SEEDS[1])
g2 <- knn_graph(s2$X, k = 12)
ed <- short_circuits(g2, s2$X, s2$truth, tau = 2)

seg <- function(P, lab) data.frame(
  panel = lab, short = ed$short,
  x  = P[ed$i, 1], y  = P[ed$i, 2],
  xend = P[ed$j, 1], yend = P[ed$j, 2]
)

segs <- rbind(seg(s2$X[, c(1, 3)], "Folded surface (x, z)"),
              seg(s2$truth,            "Exact unfolding (truth)"))
segs <- segs[order(segs$short), ]         # short circuits drawn on top

ggplot2::ggplot(segs, ggplot2::aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend,
                                   colour = short, linetype = short)) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(linewidth = 0.25) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "solid", `TRUE` = "22"),
                                 labels = c("honest edge", "short circuit")) +
  scale_color_book(end = 0.8, labels = c("honest edge", "short circuit")) +
  ggplot2::coord_equal() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

The right-hand panel is the one to read. In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the offending edges
are short and unremarkable; on the answer key they are long chords across the
sheet. No diagnostic computed from the data alone distinguishes them, which is
why short circuits are usually discovered by noticing that the embedding looks
wrong.

Push $\theta$ further and the short circuits stop being isolated. Once they are
dense enough to percolate across the corrugation direction, shortest paths can
zig-zag the whole width of the sheet at the ambient rather than the geodesic
rate, the graph metric converges to the ambient chordal metric, and Isomap
converges to `cmdscale`. That is the endpoint of the failure and it is
falsifiable: past the collapse, Isomap's curve does not merely worsen, it merges
with the linear baseline it was supposed to improve on. The result is the one
Balasubramanian and Schwartz raised against Isomap two years after it appeared
[@balasubramanian2002isomap], reproduced here with the error measured rather than
inferred from a picture.

## The $k$ that works at low $\theta$ is not the $k$ that works at high $\theta$

$k$ controls a trade-off whose balance point moves with $\theta$. Small $k$
fragments the graph on a sparse sample and inflates the polygonal-path bias;
large $k$ enlarges the neighbourhood radius, which admits more short circuits and
lets each one span more true surface distance. Neither end is safe everywhere.

```{r geo-theta-by-k, fig.height=3.2, fig.alt="Procrustes RMSE against fold angle theta, faceted into five panels for k equal to 5, 8, 12, 20 and 30. Each panel shows two curves: Isomap as a solid dark purple line with an interquartile ribbon, and the classical MDS baseline as a dashed orange line. The MDS baseline rises steadily with theta and is identical in every panel. Isomap tracks near zero error across a range of theta, then rises abruptly to meet the MDS baseline. The theta at which the rise begins is similar across panels, but the height and steepness of the jump grow with k, and at k equal to 5 the curve is truncated at low theta where the graph is fragmented."}
K_GRID <- c(5, 8, 12, 20, 30)
THETA  <- seq(0, 1.4, length.out = 15)   # theta is bounded by pi/2

rows <- list()
for (th in THETA) for (sd in BENCH_SEEDS) {
  si <- sample_manifold(pat, theta = th, n = 800, seed = sd)
  rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
    theta = th, seed = sd, k = NA_integer_, method = "classical MDS",
    rmse = reconstruction_error(cmdscale(dist(si$X), k = 2), si$truth))
  for (kk in K_GRID) {
    Y <- isomap_embed(si$X, kk)
    rows[[length(rows) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
      theta = th, seed = sd, k = kk, method = "Isomap",
      rmse = if (is.null(Y)) NA_real_ else reconstruction_error(Y, si$truth))
  }
}
cur  <- do.call(rbind, rows)

base <- subset(cur, method == "classical MDS")
base <- do.call(rbind, lapply(K_GRID, function(kk) transform(base, k = kk)))
cur  <- rbind(subset(cur, method == "Isomap"), base)

q <- aggregate(rmse ~ theta + k + method, cur, na.action = na.pass,
               FUN = function(v) c(med = median(v, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   lo  = quantile(v, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
                                   hi  = quantile(v, .75, na.rm = TRUE)))
q <- do.call(data.frame, q)
names(q)[4:6] <- c("med", "lo", "hi")

ggplot2::ggplot(q, ggplot2::aes(theta, med, colour = method, linetype = method)) +
  ggplot2::geom_ribbon(ggplot2::aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, fill = method),
                       alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ k, nrow = 1,
                      labeller = ggplot2::labeller(k = function(v) paste0("k = ", v))) +
  scale_color_book(end = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_book(end = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = expression(theta), y = "Procrustes RMSE",
                colour = NULL, fill = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

Two things follow, and both invalidate the usual reporting practice. The
ranking of $k$ reverses across the fold angle: the value that minimises RMSE on
a nearly flat sheet is among the worst once the fold is deep, so a single-$k$
evaluation reports the position of an arbitrary point on a curve whose shape it
does not show. And past a certain $\theta$ the window closes entirely — every
$k$ small enough to avoid short circuits is too small to keep the graph
connected. Beyond that angle Isomap has no admissible tuning, which is a more
useful thing to report than a best-case number.

## Where the graph first bridges

The onset can be predicted, not just observed. Two families of bad edge exist
and they have different criteria.

Take the Miura corrugation seen end-on: a triangle wave of slant length $a$,
amplitude $H(\theta) = a \sin\theta \sin\alpha$ and projected half-wavelength
$L(\theta) = a\sqrt{1 - \sin^2\theta \sin^2\alpha}$, so that $H^2 + L^2 = a^2$
[@schenk2013miura]. Write $\lambda(\theta) = L/a$ for the contraction of the
corrugation direction.

**Across a crease.** Two points at equal arclength $s$ on opposite flanks of a
valley are $2s$ apart along the surface and $2s\lambda$ apart in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, for every $s$. The configuration is scale-free, so
$\rho = 1/\lambda(\theta)$ regardless of $s$, $k$ or $n$, and short circuits of
this family appear when

$$\sin^2\theta_\star \;=\; \frac{1 - \tau^{-2}}{\sin^2\alpha}.$$

At $\alpha = \pi/3$ the fully folded sheet has $\lambda = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 60^\circ} = 1/2$
exactly, so $\rho$ tops out at exactly $2$: with $\tau = 2$ the threshold
coincides with $\theta_{\max}$, and with $\tau = 1.5$ it falls at
$\theta_\star = 1.04$. The onset of this family does not depend on $k$ at all.

**Across a trough.** Two facets separated by an intervening facet are $2L(\theta)$
apart in $\mathbb{R}^3$ at closest approach, a fixed distance rather than a
scale-free one, so they bridge when the neighbourhood radius reaches it. For $n$
points uniform on a sheet of area $A$, the expected $k$-th-neighbour distance is
$r_k = \sqrt{kA/(\pi n)}$; writing $m$ for the mean number of sample points per
facet, the criterion $2L(\theta) \le r_k$ becomes

$$\frac{k}{m} \;\ge\; \frac{4\pi\, a\, \lambda(\theta)^2}{b \sin\alpha}.$$

At $a = b = 1$, $\alpha = \pi/3$ and full compression the right-hand side is
$3.6$. With twenty points per facet this family needs $k \gtrsim 70$ and never
fires on the book's grid; with five points per facet it needs only
$k \gtrsim 20$ and does. Sample size and neighbourhood size enter here, and only
here.

```{r geo-bridge-theta}
r_k <- function(k, n, area) sqrt(k * area / (pi * n))

theta_bridge_analytic <- function(k, n, area, a = 1, alpha = pi / 3, tau = 2) {
  solve_theta <- function(s2) if (s2 <= 1) asin(sqrt(max(s2, 0))) else NA_real_
  c(crease = solve_theta((1 - tau^-2) / sin(alpha)^2),
    trough = solve_theta((1 - r_k(k, n, area)^2 / (4 * a^2)) / sin(alpha)^2))
}

theta_bridge_empirical <- function(pat, k, n, seeds, tau = 2,
                                   thetas = seq(0, 1.4, length.out = 40)) {
  vapply(seeds, function(sd) {
    for (th in thetas) {
      si <- sample_manifold(fold(pat, th), n = n, seed = sd)
      gi <- knn_graph(si$X, k)
      if (any(short_circuits(gi, si$X, si$truth, tau)$short)) return(th)
    }
    NA_real_
  }, numeric(1))
}

emp <- theta_bridge_empirical(pat, k = 12, n = 800, seeds = BENCH_SEEDS, tau = 1.5)
quantile(emp, c(.1, .5, .9))
```

Report the empirical onset as a distribution over `BENCH_SEEDS`, not a point.
The analytic threshold is where bridging pairs first *exist*; whether a
particular sample contains one is a matter of where its points fell, so the
measured onset sits at or above the prediction and tightens onto it as $n$
grows. Agreement between the two is the check that the mechanism is understood
rather than merely named.

## Spectral relatives

Laplacian eigenmaps skip the geodesic entirely. Weight each graph edge by
$w_{ij} = \exp(-\lVert x_i - x_j\rVert^2/\sigma^2)$, then minimise
$\sum_{ij} w_{ij}\lVert y_i - y_j\rVert^2$ subject to $Y^\top D Y = I$; the
solution is the generalised eigenvectors of $Ly = \gamma D y$ for the smallest
non-zero $\gamma$ [@belkin2003laplacian]. Numerically it is cleaner to work with
the symmetric conjugate $\mathcal{A} = D^{-1/2} W D^{-1/2}$ and take its largest
algebraic eigenvalues, which `RSpectra` handles directly.

```{r geo-laplacian-eigenmaps}
laplacian_eigenmap <- function(X, k = 12, d = 2, sigma = NULL) {
  g <- knn_graph(X, k)
  W <- igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g, attr = "weight", sparse = TRUE)
  if (is.null(sigma)) sigma <- mean(W@x)
  W@x <- exp(-(W@x / sigma)^2)
  dg  <- Matrix::rowSums(W)
  Dh  <- Matrix::Diagonal(x = 1 / sqrt(dg))
  e   <- RSpectra::eigs_sym(Dh %*% W %*% Dh, k = d + 1, which = "LA")
  sweep(e$vectors[, -1, drop = FALSE], 1, sqrt(dg), "/")   # drop trivial vector
}
```

Diffusion maps add two knobs to the same object [@coifman2006diffusion]. An
anisotropic normalisation $w_{ij} \mapsto w_{ij}/(q_i^\alpha q_j^\alpha)$ with
$q_i = \sum_j w_{ij}$ removes the influence of sampling density at $\alpha = 1$,
recovering the Laplace–Beltrami operator; and a diffusion time $t$ rescales the
coordinates as $\gamma_\ell^{\,t}\psi_\ell$.

```{r geo-diffusion-map}
diffusion_map <- function(X, k = 12, d = 2, alpha = 1, t = 1, sigma = NULL) {
  g <- knn_graph(X, k)
  W <- igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(g, attr = "weight", sparse = TRUE)
  if (is.null(sigma)) sigma <- mean(W@x)
  W@x <- exp(-(W@x / sigma)^2)
  q  <- Matrix::rowSums(W)
  Qa <- Matrix::Diagonal(x = q^-alpha)
  Wa <- Qa %*% W %*% Qa
  dg <- Matrix::rowSums(Wa)
  Dh <- Matrix::Diagonal(x = 1 / sqrt(dg))
  e  <- RSpectra::eigs_sym(Dh %*% Wa %*% Dh, k = d + 1, which = "LA")
  psi <- sweep(e$vectors[, -1, drop = FALSE], 1, sqrt(dg), "/")
  sweep(psi, 2, e$values[-1]^t, "*")
}
```

Both inherit the same graph and therefore the same failure, but the signature
differs. Isomap's shortest path is a minimum, so one bad edge changes a block of
the distance matrix outright; the failure arrives late and abruptly. A spectral
method averages over all paths, so a bridge with a small Gaussian weight
perturbs the operator only slightly — but it perturbs the *low* end of the
spectrum, exactly where the informative eigenvectors live, and the eigenvector
that the corrugation direction generates is the one a cross-fold bridge attacks.
The result is a degradation that begins earlier and rises more smoothly, and
whose visible form is not a contraction but a fold-over: the two bridged regions
map to the same place, and the eigenvalue ordering swaps, so the second and
third coordinates trade roles part-way along the $\theta$ curve. Report which
eigenvectors you used, or the curve is uninterpretable.

There is also a failure with nothing to do with folding, and this benchmark
provokes it if the sheet is set up carelessly. On a rectangle
$[0, L_x] \times [0, L_y]$ the Neumann Laplacian eigenfunctions are
$\cos(m\pi x/L_x)\cos(n\pi y/L_y)$ with eigenvalues
$\pi^2(m^2/L_x^2 + n^2/L_y^2)$. The mode $(2,0)$ precedes $(0,1)$ whenever
$L_x > 2L_y$, in which case the first two non-trivial eigenvectors are *both*
functions of $x$ and the "two-dimensional embedding" is a parabolic arc carrying
no transverse information at all. This happens at $\theta = 0$, on a perfectly
flat sheet, and it is a property of the domain rather than of the data. Keep
$n_x a$ and $n_y b$ within a factor of two of each other, or the folding results
will be contaminated by an artefact of the aspect ratio.

## What the family shares

Four methods, one graph, one point of failure. The metric each of them is trying
to estimate does not change with $\theta$, so their $\theta$-curves measure
nothing but the quality of the ambient nearest-neighbour search as an
approximation to the surface. That approximation degrades for a reason that is
now stated exactly: facets approach in $\mathbb{R}^3$ at a rate
$\lambda(\theta)$ fixed by the crease geometry, and the graph starts crossing
between them when the neighbourhood radius $r_k$ catches up.

Isomap is the sharpest case because its two stages separate cleanly and one of
them contributes zero error. It is also, on this benchmark, the method with the
best claim to being fair-tested: it was designed for exactly the isometric
setting a rigid fold provides, given the geodesics it recovers the answer key to
machine precision, and it still fails — not because the premise was wrong, but
because the graph that estimates the geodesics is built in the wrong space.

Chapter \@ref(neighbor) takes the same graph to methods that make no metric
claim at all, and Chapter \@ref(evaluation) asks whether the quantities usually
used to certify these embeddings would have caught any of this.
